cards.title: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood
cards.body:
An octopus runs on three hearts. Two branchial hearts pump blood through the gills, where it picks up oxygen, and a third, the systemic heart, pushes it around the rest of the body. Curiously, the systemic heart stops beating while the octopus swims, one reason octopuses tend to prefer crawling: swimming is exhausting.

Their blood is blue because it carries oxygen using hemocyanin, a copper-based protein, instead of the iron-based hemoglobin that makes ours red. Hemocyanin works well in cold, low-oxygen water but carries less oxygen overall, which helps explain the need for extra pumping power.

And that's just the plumbing. Around two-thirds of an octopus's neurons sit in its arms, which can taste what they touch and react with surprising independence from the central brain.
cards.example: Octopuses and humans last shared an ancestor more than 500 million years ago, likely a simple worm-like creature. So the octopus's problem-solving intelligence evolved almost entirely separately from ours, with a very different body plan built around it.
cards.takeaway: Octopuses solved intelligence and circulation in a completely alien way.

cards.title: Margin of safety: Graham's three-word secret
cards.body:
In the final chapter of The Intelligent Investor, Benjamin Graham set himself the challenge of distilling sound investing into three words. His answer: margin of safety. Buy only when the price sits well below your estimate of intrinsic value, so that even if you're wrong, you don't lose much.

The logic is engineering, not optimism. A bridge built to hold exactly the heaviest expected truck fails on the first overloaded day; one built with a large buffer survives surprises. Your valuation will always be uncertain, because forecasts of growth, margins and discount rates are educated guesses. The discount to value is your buffer for those errors.

How large a margin you need depends on the uncertainty. A stable business you understand well may justify a smaller one; a speculative one may need far more, or a pass.
cards.example: You value a stock at $60 per share. With a one-third margin of safety, you'd buy at $40 or less. If your estimate turns out 25% too optimistic, true value is $45 and you're still ahead. Buying at $58 leaves no room for that same mistake.
cards.takeaway: Pay a price low enough that being wrong doesn't ruin you.

cards.title: The IKEA effect: we overvalue what we build
cards.body:
People place extra value on things they've made themselves, even when the result is mediocre. In research published in 2012, Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon and Dan Ariely had participants assemble simple IKEA storage boxes. They were willing to pay noticeably more for their own boxes than for identical pre-assembled ones, and in another test rated their amateur origami almost as highly as an expert's.

Effort creates attachment. That's useful, since people stick with projects they've invested in, but it distorts judgment. We overrate our own ideas, plans and spreadsheets simply because we built them.

Investors are especially exposed. After weeks building a detailed model and thesis, it's painful to admit the stock is a bad idea. Guard against it by writing down, before you start, what evidence would make you abandon the idea, and by asking someone uninvolved to attack it.
cards.example: You've spent a month on a model showing a stock is worth $80. New data cuts your revenue forecast by 15%. The IKEA effect will push you to hunt for reasons the model still works. Instead, update the numbers first, then decide what you think.
cards.takeaway: Effort breeds attachment; judge your own work as if a stranger made it.

cards.title: Chickpea Shakshuka with Feta
cards.body:
Shakshuka, eggs poached in a spiced tomato sauce, is popular across North Africa and the Middle East, and adding chickpeas turns it into a serious protein meal. In a large skillet, soften a diced onion and a red pepper in 1 tbsp olive oil for about 6 minutes. Add 3 cloves of garlic, 2 tsp paprika, 1 tsp cumin and a pinch of chili flakes, and stir for a minute.

Pour in a 796 mL can of crushed tomatoes and a drained 540 mL can of chickpeas, and simmer for 10 minutes until thick. Make six wells in the sauce, crack an egg into each, cover, and cook on low for 6 to 8 minutes until the whites set but the yolks stay soft.

Scatter with 60 g of crumbled feta and fresh parsley, and serve straight from the pan.
cards.example: Makes 2 servings at roughly 33 g protein each: about 18 g from three eggs, 11 g from half the chickpeas and 4 g from the feta. Serve with toasted whole-grain bread to mop up the sauce and add a few more grams.
cards.takeaway: Eggs plus chickpeas turn shakshuka into a 30 g protein dinner.

cards.title: Network effects: why winners take most
cards.body:
A product has network effects when it becomes more valuable as more people use it. A phone is useless if no one else has one; a marketplace with more buyers attracts more sellers, which in turn attracts more buyers.

The number of possible connections grows much faster than the number of users. With n users there are n(n − 1)/2 possible pairs, so 10 users give 45 connections but 1,000 users give nearly 500,000. That's why markets with strong network effects often tip toward one or two dominant players.

There are different kinds. Direct effects come from users connecting with each other, as in messaging apps. Two-sided effects link different groups, like a card network connecting cardholders and merchants. The catch is the cold-start problem: a network is nearly worthless when empty, so early growth is brutally hard and often subsidized.
cards.example: Visa and Mastercard are classic two-sided networks: merchants accept them because nearly every consumer carries one, and consumers carry them because nearly every merchant accepts them. A new card network would struggle to convince either side to move first.
cards.takeaway: Network effects make products more valuable with each user, so markets tip.

cards.title: Why English spelling makes so little sense
cards.body:
English spelling looks chaotic partly because it froze while pronunciation kept moving. Between roughly 1400 and 1700, the Great Vowel Shift changed how long vowels were pronounced. In Chaucer's time, time sounded more like "teem" and house more like "hoose".

At the same time, printing arrived. William Caxton set up England's first printing press in 1476, and printers gradually standardized spellings that often reflected older pronunciations. The letters stayed put while the sounds moved on.

Other quirks came from deliberate tinkering. Scholars added silent letters to show Latin roots, like the b in debt, from Latin debitum, even though English had borrowed the word from French as dette. And the k in knight and knee was once pronounced, which is why the words are spelled that way.
cards.example: Try reading the opening line of Chaucer's Canterbury Tales aloud: "Whan that Aprill with his shoures soote." Shoures (showers) was pronounced closer to "shoo-res". Many modern spellings still preserve sounds like these, centuries after speech moved on.
cards.takeaway: English spelling records how words sounded centuries ago, not today.

quiz.question: Why is octopus blood blue?
options: It contains chlorophyll
It carries oxygen with copper-based hemocyanin
It contains no oxygen at all
Seawater dyes it blue
quiz.explanation: Hemocyanin uses copper instead of iron to bind oxygen, which gives the blood a blue colour.

quiz.question: You value a stock at $90. To buy with a one-third margin of safety, what's the most you'd pay?
quiz.explanation: A one-third discount to $90 is $30, so the maximum price is $60.

quiz.question: Which habit best protects an analyst from the IKEA effect?
options: Writing down in advance what evidence would make them abandon the thesis
Spending more time refining the model
Only reading reports that agree with them
Adding to the position after more research
quiz.explanation: Pre-committing to kill criteria counters the attachment that effort creates.

quiz.question: In the chickpea shakshuka, how are the eggs cooked?
options: Scrambled into the sauce at the start
Hard-boiled separately and sliced on top
Cracked into wells in the sauce and poached under a lid
Baked into a crust
quiz.explanation: The eggs are cracked into wells in the simmering sauce and cooked covered until the whites set.

quiz.question: Review: What combination of conditions defined 1970s stagflation?
options: Low inflation and low unemployment
High inflation alongside rising unemployment
Falling prices and rapid growth
Low interest rates and a housing boom
quiz.explanation: Stagflation combined double-digit inflation with rising unemployment, breaking the simple Phillips curve trade-off.

quiz.question: Why does English spelling often not match pronunciation?
options: Dictionaries were written by non-English speakers
Victorian reformers randomized spellings
Pronunciation hasn't changed since Chaucer
Spellings were standardized with printing while vowel sounds kept shifting
quiz.explanation: Printing fixed spellings during and after the Great Vowel Shift, so spelling reflects older pronunciations.
